{"id": "3:49/q05", "question": "To whom was Jesus sent, and how broad was his mission?", "turns_on": "Whether all Israel, only a subset, or a particular mission within wider prophethood.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q05/p1", "position": "His commission was to all the Children of Israel.", "reasons": "Jishumī, al-Ṭabrisī, Rāzī and Kur'an Yolu explicitly oppose the claim that he addressed only a particular Israelite group."}, {"id": "3:49/q05/p2", "position": "He was sent only to a particular Israelite group.", "reasons": "Some Jews are said to claim this; Bayḍāwī gives a limited-commission possibility."}, {"id": "3:49/q05/p3", "position": "The wording rebuts a claim that Jesus was sent to non-Israelites.", "reasons": "Bayḍāwī and an unattributed report offer this; al-Ālūsī doubts the alleged Jewish claim, finding it absent from familiar Jewish books."}, {"id": "3:49/q05/p4", "position": "His special messenger mission was to Israel, while prophethood could reach other peoples.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī distinguishes particular messengership from conveying religion generally; he cites Moses's address to Pharaoh and Jesus's acceptance among Romans, eastern peoples, and Najrān."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q06", "question": "How does Jesus's Israelite mission relate to Torah law?", "turns_on": "Retaining earlier law with some abrogation.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q06/p1", "position": "He confirmed and taught Torah law while making some prohibitions lawful.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya mentions certain foods, camel meat, fish and birds; al-Qushayrī and Jishumī say some rulings were retained and some abrogated."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q07", "question": "Who was the first and last prophet of Israel in the reports?", "turns_on": "Reports differ between Joseph and Moses for the first.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q07/p1", "position": "Joseph was first and Jesus last.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī asserts this; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī report it."}, {"id": "3:49/q07/p2", "position": "Moses was first and Jesus last.", "reasons": "A report attributed to the Prophet in Jishumī says this; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī also note Moses as an alternative."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q08", "question": "What minor vocal or sound variants occur in the opening words?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q08/p1", "position": "The hamza of Isrāʾīl and the first-person suffix have dialectal variants without changed sense.", "reasons": "Qirāʾāt ER records both the base pronoun vocalization and a dialectal suffix variant, plus a change in the glottal stop of Isrāʾīl."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q09", "question": "Whose speech is 'I have come to you' and how does it enter the narrative?", "turns_on": "Where angelic announcement ends and Jesus's later speech begins.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q09/p1", "position": "The angels tell Mary what Jesus will later say to Israel.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān carry the announcement onward; the transition to Jesus's speech is understood after 'Israel'."}, {"id": "3:49/q09/p2", "position": "The narrative shifts to Jesus's later direct address to Israel.", "reasons": "Asad prefers this on the narrative movement from 3:52; al-Ṭabrisī says Jesus addressed them when sent."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q10", "question": "How is the first annī in 'I have come' read and governed?", "turns_on": "Open hamza attaches the clause; broken hamza resumes or quotes speech.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q10/p1", "position": "With fatḥa, it depends on messengerhood or an implied bi or li.", "reasons": "Al-Kisāʾī relates it to sending; Sībawayh and al-Farrāʾ delete bi; al-Naḥḥās treats anna as accusative; Ibn ʿĀshūr hears the declaration accompanying the mission."}, {"id": "3:49/q10/p2", "position": "A kasra reading begins direct speech or a fresh assertion.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj and Ibn Khālawayh allow an implied saying or new sentence; Qirāʾāt ER describes the independent assertion."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q11", "question": "What does 'a sign' denote here, and why is it singular?", "turns_on": "Whether it names bird-making specifically or a class/unity of multiple miracles.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q11/p1", "position": "It is proof of Jesus's prophethood and truthful mission, embracing the listed miracles.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Isḥāq, Rāzī and others call it evidence; al-Baghawī says many signs establish one truth; al-Ālūsī says indefiniteness magnifies it; Rāzī treats the singular as generic."}, {"id": "3:49/q11/p2", "position": "The singular sign is specifically the clay bird; later cures form a new sentence.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī explicitly parses the bird miracle as the sign and the other wonders as subsequent discourse."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q12", "question": "Is 'sign' read in the singular or plural?", "turns_on": "The canonical singular is generic; Ibn Masʿūd's plural expresses the number of acts.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q12/p1", "position": "The common text has singular āya in both occurrences.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn take singular as a collective or generic designation."}, {"id": "3:49/q12/p2", "position": "Ibn Masʿūd or ʿAbd Allāh reads plural āyāt in both places.", "reasons": "This directly reflects the multiple signs."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q13", "question": "How does 'with a sign' attach to 'I have come'?", "turns_on": "Whether a direct complement or a circumstantial accompaniment.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q13/p1", "position": "It attaches to 'I have come', with bāʾ marking accompaniment or transitivity.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī gives both uses; Ibn ʿĀshūr emphasizes Jesus's status as messenger while taking the bāʾ as accompaniment."}, {"id": "3:49/q13/p2", "position": "It is a circumstantial phrase: Jesus came bearing a sign.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn allows an omitted general predicate, but rejects Abū al-Baqāʾ's specific implied 'advancing'."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q14", "question": "How does the following 'to make lawful' clause relate to 'I came with a sign'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q14/p1", "position": "It is coordinated with Jesus's coming: he came with a sign and to make some things lawful.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf links the following wa-li-uḥilla back to bi-āyatin min rabbikum."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q15", "question": "What does 'from your Lord' modify, and why say 'your Lord'?", "turns_on": "Whether it qualifies the sign or the coming.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q15/p1", "position": "It attaches to 'I have come': Jesus came from God with the sign.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī allow this; al-Biqāʿī and al-Ālūsī say 'your Lord' evokes beneficence and obedience."}, {"id": "3:49/q15/p2", "position": "It qualifies the sign as having its figurative origin with God.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn posit an omitted relational phrase; al-Ālūsī calls min figurative origin."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q16", "question": "Why does the speech shift between singular and plural address?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q16/p1", "position": "The shift shows the sign is witnessed and beneficial both individually and collectively.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says it answers doubts that only a group could witness it or that it benefits just one person."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q17", "question": "How is 'that I create' read and parsed?", "turns_on": "Fatḥa subordinates the explanatory clause; kasra can resume it or explain the sign.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q17/p1", "position": "Kasra: it is an independent assertion or explanatory quotation of the sign.", "reasons": "Nāfiʿ is commonly named, with Abū Jaʿfar added by Ibn ʿĀshūr and the two Medinans by Ibn al-Jazarī; al-Wāḥidī, al-Ṭabrisī and Rāzī prefer the explanatory link, citing 5:9, 3:59 or 48:29."}, {"id": "3:49/q17/p2", "position": "Fatḥa: the clause apposes the first annī or the sign, or predicates an omitted 'it is'.", "reasons": "Al-Fārisī reports all but Nāfiʿ opening it; grammarians variously make it accusative, genitive, or nominative. Abū al-Baqāʾ also supplies 'I mean'."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q18", "question": "What does 'I create' mean in Jesus's claim?", "turns_on": "Whether khalq here is shaping measured material or origination from nonexistence.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q18/p1", "position": "Jesus measures and shapes existing clay into a bird likeness.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī's successors cite craft usage, Zuhayr and other poetry, a measured sandal, and 29:17 and 23:14 for nonabsolute uses. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls proportioning the root sense and distinguishes originating an animal."}, {"id": "3:49/q18/p2", "position": "Khalq can also mean bringing an entity from nonexistence, a sense reserved for God.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān distinguishes the two senses; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says bodily origination properly belongs to God, while figurative khalq covers fabricating falsehood at 29:17."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q19", "question": "Can a human be called a creator or originator on the evidence of this verse?", "turns_on": "The scope of human agency and the divine name al-Khāliq.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q19/p1", "position": "A servant can be called creator only in a qualified sense of forming or originating an act; God alone is Creator absolutely.", "reasons": "Jishumī and al-Ṭabrisī use the verse against the Mujbira; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites 'best of creators' at 23:14. Ibn ʿAṭiyya distinguishes Jesus's shaping from God's origination of life."}, {"id": "3:49/q19/p2", "position": "The divine name al-Khāliq belongs only to God.", "reasons": "Rāzī reports his school's appeal to 13:16 and 35:3, while he rejects treating 35:3 alone as decisive because its negation includes providing from heaven."}, {"id": "3:49/q19/p3", "position": "Al-Khāliq is not literally a divine name if it implies conjectural measuring.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAbd Allāh al-Baṣrī advances this objection; Rāzī's school answers that measuring can mean knowledge without conjecture."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q20", "question": "Was the bird miracle requested by challengers?", "turns_on": "Public demand versus an offered sign at

Abū Ḥayyān finds no demand apparent from the verse."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q21", "question": "When did Jesus first animate the clay bird?", "turns_on": "Schoolboy story versus challenge upon claiming prophethood.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q21/p1", "position": "As a boy in a scribal school.", "reasons": "Ibn Isḥāq says the other boys witnessed it, publicized it, and Mary later fled."}, {"id": "3:49/q21/p2", "position": "After he claimed prophethood, as a challenge from the Israelites.", "reasons": "Rāzī, al-Bursawī and al-Ālūsī report the request for a bat."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q22", "question": "What other grammatical scope and ordering details are noted in the miracle clauses?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q22/p1", "position": "The coordinated healing and revival clauses remain within the scope of annī and its predicates.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī state their syntactic dependence."}, {"id": "3:49/q22/p2", "position": "The imperfect verbs portray repeated acts and are ordered from the greatest creative sign through healing, revival, and disclosure.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn emphasize recurring action; Abū Ḥayyān identifies creation as the foremost miracle."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q23", "question": "Why does Jesus say 'for you'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q23/p1", "position": "The shaping serves the audience's benefit by inviting faith and ending denial.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says it qualifies his limited shaping; al-Samīn calls the lām purposive, and al-Bursawī specifies faith as the purpose."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q24", "question": "What is the clay and what does 'from clay' contribute?", "turns_on": "Its physical sense and whether min limits the material source.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q24/p1", "position": "It is ordinary clay, water and earth that can receive a shape; min marks its starting material.", "reasons": "Jishumī and al-Ṭabrisī cite sealing a document or coating a house; al-Ḥarālī describes matured water and earth. Abū Ḥayyān says the source material excludes ex nihilo creation; al-Samīn rejects a merely explanatory min."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q25", "question": "What does the clay-bird miracle show beyond Jesus's truthfulness?", "turns_on": "The notes give distinct emphases on divine life, resurrection, Adam, and Jesus's birth.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q25/p1", "position": "It displays God's power to create life and resurrect whatever He wills.", "reasons": "Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmits Ibn Isḥāq; al-Biqāʿī says power over some dead proves power over all and compares Adam."}, {"id": "3:49/q25/p2", "position": "It parallels Jesus's own unusual birth, which should not suggest his divinity.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī links it to the fatherless birth; al-Biqāʿī says Adam's dust creation is still more astonishing."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q26", "question": "What minor lexical and grammatical details accompany the bird narrative?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q26/p1", "position": "The result becomes a living bird, while the clay term has related Arabic forms and names.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān notes the transmitter nicknamed Muṭīn; al-Samīn says ilā Banī Isrāʾīl can depend on rasūl or be its omitted adjective. The bird is truly living, as al-Kashshāf explains."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q27", "question": "How does the comparison 'like the form' work syntactically?", "turns_on": "Whether kāf is a noun object, modifies an omitted object, or modifies an omitted verbal noun.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q27/p1", "position": "Kāf or its phrase modifies an omitted object: Jesus makes something shaped like a bird.", "reasons": "Most grammarians and al-Samīn favor this; Ibn ʿĀshūr takes the object from 'I create'."}, {"id": "3:49/q27/p2", "position": "Kāf itself is a noun meaning 'likeness' and direct object.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash and Abū al-Ḥasan permit this; al-Samīn says other grammarians restrict a noun-like kāf to necessity."}, {"id": "3:49/q27/p3", "position": "Kāf modifies an omitted verbal noun: I create a creation like a bird's form.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAlī proposes this; al-Samīn objects that the challenge concerns the created result, unless the verbal noun means its object."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q28", "question": "What does hayʾa mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether a state, form, or verbal noun for its formed result.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q28/p1", "position": "The prepared visible shape or configuration of a bird.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj and al-Baghawī derive it from preparation or setting right; al-Ḥarālī describes the arrangement of limbs; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it a clay image."}, {"id": "3:49/q28/p2", "position": "A verbal noun transferred to the thing prepared.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn compares khalq for a created thing; al-Ālūsī contrasts the verbal-noun analysis with a noun of state or a boundary-defined quality."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q29", "question": "How is hayʾa read and pronounced?", "turns_on": "Hamza retained versus its vowel transferred to a doubled yāʾ.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q29/p1", "position": "A variant eases hamza to a doubled yāʾ, hayya.", "reasons": "Al-Zuhrī, Abū Jaʿfar, al-Aʿraj and others are named across reports; al-Samīn calls it eloquent, while Qirāʾāt ER notes no semantic change."}, {"id": "3:49/q29/p2", "position": "The common reading retains hamza after the silent yāʾ.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it the reading of all readers; some accounts distinguish the main text from al-Zuhrī and Abū Jaʿfar's eased form."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q30", "question": "What bird did Jesus fashion, and what happened to it?", "turns_on": "Bat only versus several birds, and whether it died after leaving view.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q30/p1", "position": "He fashioned a bat, presented as the hardest or most remarkable bird.", "reasons": "Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Isḥāq say people chose it because it is flesh without feathers; later reports add teeth, breasts, ears, live birth, milk, menstruation, laughter, and twilight vision. Some say he made no other kind."}, {"id": "3:49/q30/p2", "position": "The bird flew while watched, then fell dead out of sight.", "reasons": "Wahb's report distinguishes Jesus's craft from God's unmediated, enduring creation. Some place the episode at school, others amid challengers."}, {"id": "3:49/q30/p3", "position": "The clay likeness became a living flying bird like other birds.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf, Bayḍāwī and al-Ālūsī stress that the resulting bird truly flew by God's leave."}, {"id": "3:49/q30/p4", "position": "He fashioned multiple birds or several kinds.", "reasons": "The plural reading and repeated action support this for al-Ṭabarī, al-Thaʿlabī and others; al-Ālūsī reports this against the bat-only view."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q31", "question": "What does al-ṭayr mean, and how is it read in 'form of the bird'?", "turns_on": "Collective ṭayr versus singular active participle ṭāʾir, and the lexical scope of ṭayr.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q31/p1", "position": "The common al-ṭayr is a collective bird species, usable for one or many.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī calls it plural of ṭāʾir; Abū al-Ḥasan and Sībawayh call it collective, with regular plurals aṭyār and ṭuyūr. Al-Akhfash treats it as plural like rukb."}, {"id": "3:49/q31/p2", "position": "Abū Jaʿfar and others read singular al-ṭāʾir, naming one bird or a genus.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya say the first singular can be generic; al-Nashr says Abū Jaʿfar uses it in both places and notes hamza transmission."}, {"id": "3:49/q31/p3", "position": "Ṭayr can also mean flying itself or, by usage, destiny or fortune.", "reasons": "Asad cites 7:131, 27:47, 36:19 and 17:13, supporting his parabolic reading of the bird sign."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q32", "question": "What is the blowing, and what can it act upon grammatically?", "turns_on": "Ordinary breath through the mouth versus theological inference about spirit; preposition retained or deleted.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q32/p1", "position": "Nafkh is forcefully expelling air or breath into the fashioned figure.", "reasons": "Jishumī defines air from the mouth; al-Ḥarālī says forceful sending from its source; al-Nābigha's poetic construction can omit fī."}, {"id": "3:49/q32/p2", "position": "The breath indicates spirit as a subtle, windlike body.", "reasons": "Jishumī and some theologians infer this from the wording; Rāzī compares Gabriel's breath into Mary."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q33", "question": "Are there other readings of 'I breathe into it'?", "turns_on": "Masculine with fī versus feminine direct object.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q33/p1", "position": "The ordinary reading has masculine fīhi.", "reasons": "Its antecedent can be the formed thing, a bird, or clay; 5:110 uses feminine agreement with hayʾa."}, {"id": "3:49/q33/p2", "position": "A rare reading has fa-anfukh-hā without fī.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ transmits it, al-Kashshāf attributes it to ʿAbd Allāh; the feminine refers to hayʾa. Al-Ṭabarī and al-Samīn cite Arabic and poetry for direct-object nafkh."}]}

{"id": "3:49/q38", "question": "What does 'by God's permission' mean for the miracles?", "turns_on": "Whether permission is knowledge and enabling, command, or God's creating the result.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q38/p1", "position": "God Himself brings the life or healing into being when Jesus prays or breathes.", "reasons": "Rāzī cites 3:145, 67:2 and 2:258; Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Ṭabrisī say God originates life, while Jesus visibly shapes and supplicates. Al-Ālūsī says any breath could be its occasion by divine will."}, {"id": "3:49/q38/p2", "position": "God authorizes and enables the act, knowing it will occur.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya compares 2:251 and the report on silence as consent; Abū Ḥayyān combines enabling and knowledge."}, {"id": "3:49/q38/p3", "position": "It means God's command or power.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī and al-Nasafī use command; al-Ṭabrisī distinguishes human shaping and breathing from divine creation of living flesh."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q39", "question": "Why is 'by God's permission' repeated and placed after bird-making and resurrection?", "turns_on": "Avoiding deification; whether omission after healing and knowledge is coordinated scope or a meaningful distinction.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q39/p1", "position": "The repetition attributes astonishing life-giving acts to God and prevents deifying Jesus.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf, Rāzī, Bayḍāwī, al-Biqāʿī, Ibn ʿĀshūr and others explicitly counter claims of Jesus's divinity; al-Biqāʿī compares Adam's dust creation."}, {"id": "3:49/q39/p2", "position": "The phrase is stated after the two greatest miracles; coordination extends its force to healing and foretelling.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān says creation and resurrection are greatest and the others attach to them; al-Samīn stresses the qualifier after creation and revival."}, {"id": "3:49/q39/p3", "position": "Knowledge and healing omit the phrase because Jesus performs the speech or the healing is already framed as God's sign.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī distinguishes the spoken report from acts God truly creates, cites 13:38, and says explicit sign language suffices for healing."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q40", "question": "What does 'by God's permission' attach to in the bird clause?", "turns_on": "Whether the phrase modifies being, the bird description, or the whole miracle.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q40/p1", "position": "It modifies yakūn, the bird's becoming.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and Abū al-Baqāʾ permit this; al-Samīn says it is clearest if kāna is complete."}, {"id": "3:49/q40/p2", "position": "It modifies ṭayran or ṭāʾiran, describing the bird as enabled by God.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn allows an omitted relation with collective ṭayr and direct modification of singular ṭāʾiran; Abū Ḥayyān permits this too."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q41", "question": "What does 'I heal' mean, and how is the verb formed?", "turns_on": "The sources vary dialect attributions for bariʾa and baraʾa.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q41/p1", "position": "Jesus removes illness and restores a patient to health.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī cites Arabic usage for both recovery forms; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says a patient is healed and another heals him; al-Ḥarālī describes full release from impaired faculties."}, {"id": "3:49/q41/p2", "position": "Tamīm uses bariʾtu and Ḥijāz uses baraʾtu.", "reasons": "Al-Aṣmaʿī gives this attribution; al-Rāghib extends both vowels to illness while debt and sin take fatḥa."}, {"id": "3:49/q41/p3", "position": "The regional attribution is reversed for baraʾtu.", "reasons": "Abū Zayd says the rest of the Arabs use bariʾtu."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q42", "question": "How did Jesus treat the crowds of sick people, according to reports?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q42/p1", "position": "As many as fifty thousand came in a day; he went to those unable to reach him and healed by prayer, often conditional on faith.", "reasons": "Wahb is repeatedly cited; versions vary on whether he also touched patients. Al-Bursawī reports some believed and others called it magic; al-Ālūsī quotes the prayer and a use for fear or mental illness."}, {"id": "3:49/q42/p2", "position": "Galen and colleagues held congenital blindness and advanced baras incurable.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī reports their medical judgment; Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān repeat a historical story that Galen died traveling to meet Jesus."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q43", "question": "Who is al-akmah?", "turns_on": "The decisive issue is whether the word indicates congenital or absolute blindness, lesser sight loss, or a figurative incapacity.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q43/p1", "position": "A person born blind, often described as never seeing light or having closed/erased eyes.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatāda recur; Ruʾba and Suwayd are cited for blindness. Al-Ṭabarī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefer this because ordinary treatment cannot restore congenital sight, making the sign conclusive; Ibn Kathīr agrees."}, {"id": "3:49/q43/p2", "position": "A blind person generally, whether born blind or losing sight later.", "reasons": "Qatāda, al-Ḥasan, al-Suddī and others give the broad gloss; al-Khalīl and al-Rāghib allow acquired blindness. Al-Ṭabarī cites Suwayd and Ruʾba; Ibn ʿĀshūr allows both."}, {"id": "3:49/q43/p3", "position": "A person who sees by day but not at night.", "reasons": "Mujāhid is the repeated authority, with al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Ikrima and al-Aʿmash in some sources. {"id": "3:49/q44", "question": "What grammatical form links al-akmah and al-abraṣ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q44/p1", "position": "Both are afʿal adjectives for defects or disease, whose feminine is faʿlāʾ.", "reasons": "Sībawayh distinguishes afʿal color and defect patterns, their verbs and verbal nouns, and examples such as aʿwar/ʿawrāʾ; he notes irregular amyal and other neighboring patterns."}]}

{"id": "3:49/q47", "question": "What legal implication is drawn from leprosy?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q47/p1", "position": "Some Muslim jurists counted baras as a spousal defect permitting annulment, though descriptions were imprecise.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr notes this alongside the disease's stigma."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q48", "question": "What does Jesus's 'I revive the dead' mean, and who performs it?", "turns_on": "Literal temporary revival by God's answer to prayer versus inward revival of the spiritually dead.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q48/p1", "position": "God literally revived dead persons in answer to Jesus's prayer; the plural suggests several.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, Jishumī and al-Ṭabrisī attribute life to God; Dāmghānī says it preceded final resurrection without lasting worldly sustenance; Ibn ʿĀshūr cites a Gospel girl. {"id": "3:49/q49", "question": "How did Jesus raise the dead according to reports, and how reliable are the reports?", "turns_on": "Prayer formulas and actions differ; two prayer-cycle report is judged weak.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q49/p1", "position": "He prayed to God, sometimes invoking 'O Living, O Sustainer' or the greatest name.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbī and others give yā ḥayyu yā qayyūm; Sam's revival is linked to the greatest name. {"id": "3:49/q50", "question": "Whom did Jesus revive in the reports?", "turns_on": "Different named people, count, and later survival.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q50/p1", "position": "Sām son of Noah rose gray-haired, spoke, then died again.", "reasons": "Accounts vary on the divine name invoked, how long he had been dead, and whether half his hair whitened from fearing the Hour. Some believed; others called it magic."}, {"id": "3:49/q50/p2", "position": "A widow's or old woman's son rose from a bier and lived.", "reasons": "Reports add that he dressed, carried the bier home, and later had children."}, {"id": "3:49/q50/p3", "position": "Four are named: Lazarus or al-ʿĀdhir, a widow's son, a tax collector's daughter, and Sām son of Noah.", "reasons": "The main reports say the first three lived and had children, while Sām returned to death. {"id": "3:49/q51", "question": "What does 'I inform you' promise?", "turns_on": "Literal hidden household facts versus inward meanings of consumption and storage.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q51/p1", "position": "Jesus discloses concealed facts about their food and stores, without witnessing them.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī, al-Biqāʿī and Ibn ʿĀshūr stress the concealed nature of household facts; al-Kalbī says people challenged him after other miracles. {"id": "3:49/q52", "question": "When and in what setting did the disclosure occur?", "turns_on": "Childhood school, a later challenge, or the heavenly table.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q52/p1", "position": "It began while Jesus played or studied with children.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī, Saʿīd, Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʾ and Ibn Isḥāq recur; Jesus anticipated lessons and named hidden food or fathers' deeds; parents called him a sorcerer."}, {"id": "3:49/q52/p2", "position": "It occurred when the heavenly table descended and people hid forbidden leftovers.", "reasons": "Qatāda and ʿAmmār supply the command not to save any for tomorrow; Jesus exposed breach of the covenant."}, {"id": "3:49/q52/p3", "position": "After Jesus raised the dead, people asked for a new sign about their meals and stores.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbī and later narrations say they first called resurrection magic; Jesus then disclosed midday and evening meals."}, {"id": "3:49/q52/p4", "position": "Both the childhood and table episodes may have occurred.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī explicitly allows both while treating the literal two household facts as the verse's apparent sense."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q53", "question": "What happened to the hidden schoolboys or disobedient eaters in the reports?", "turns_on": "Accounts differ over pigs alone versus apes and pigs, and whether boys or table followers were transformed.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q53/p1", "position": "Parents hid the boys, and Jesus said they would become pigs; they did.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī says the boys were hidden while their parents lied and called Jesus a sorcerer; Mary fled toward Egypt afterward. Some versions say parents called the boys pigs before Jesus confirmed it."}, {"id": "3:49/q53/p2", "position": "They became apes and pigs after Jesus's prayer or after violating the table command.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAmr's schoolboy report and ʿAmmār's table report give the pair; the latter links fear and betrayal to 5:115."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q54", "question": "Why is the disclosure a prophetic sign rather than ordinary divination?", "turns_on": "Direct divine disclosure versus inference from instruments, helpers or prior questions.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q54/p1", "position": "Jesus receives sure unseen knowledge directly from God, without instruments or trickery.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī contrasts astrologers' tools and spirit helpers; Rāzī says astrologers need questions and err. Al-Ālūsī distinguishes jafr and astrology as inference or probability, whereas revelation and inspiration are bestowed."}, {"id": "3:49/q54/p2", "position": "The disclosed fact can be humanly discoverable in principle, but the prophet obtains it by an inaccessible means.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says a proof need not involve logically unreachable facts; no stratagem explains this disclosure."}, {"id": "3:49/q54/p3", "position": "Joseph's foretelling of food may be a comparable prophetic sign.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reads 'its interpretation' in Joseph's story as referring to the food before arrival, supported by some Imāmī reports."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q55", "question": "Which food and stores does Jesus identify?", "turns_on": "Ordinary household provisions versus food from the heavenly table.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q55/p1", "position": "Their ordinary household meals and what they saved for later.", "reasons": "Mujāhid and al-Rabīʿ specify last night's meal; al-Wāḥidī and others morning food and what remained for evening; al-Ḥasan adds fear of not receiving replacement."}, {"id": "3:49/q55/p2", "position": "Food taken from the heavenly table, especially what they were forbidden to save.", "reasons": "Qatāda and ʿAmmār connect it to the table; disobedient eaters hoarded food and were transformed, with 5:115 cited."}, {"id": "3:49/q55/p3", "position": "Specific personal facts stand for all kinds of u

{"id": "3:49/q56", "question": "How does mā work in 'what you eat and what you store'?", "turns_on": "Relative noun, verbal-noun particle, or indefinite noun described by a clause.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q56/p1", "position": "Both instances are relative pronouns: the things eaten and stored.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj, al-Ṭabrisī and Abū Ḥayyān prefer this; the omitted resumptive pronouns are understood."}, {"id": "3:49/q56/p2", "position": "Both can be verbal-noun particles: your eating and storing.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās, Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Samīn allow this; most grammarians say this option requires no resumptive pronoun."}, {"id": "3:49/q56/p3", "position": "Both can be indefinite nouns with following adjectival clauses.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī allow this, with an omitted resumptive pronoun."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q57", "question": "What does 'you store' mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q57/p1", "position": "You hide or retain something for a later need, especially food.", "reasons": "Muqātil glosses next-day savings; Jishumī gives future need; al-Ḥarālī distinguishes private storing from ihtikār for trade profit. {"id": "3:49/q58", "question": "How is taddakhirūn formed, and how is it read?", "turns_on": "Assimilated dāl, simple dhāl, doubled dhāl, and unassimilated dhāl-dāl.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q58/p1", "position": "The common taddakhirūn has doubled dāl from iftiʿāl of dhakhara.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ, al-Zajjāj, al-Khalīl, Sībawayh and later grammarians explain voicing t to d beside voiced dhāl and assimilation. {"id": "3:49/q59", "question": "Why mention the house and what does 'in your houses' attach to?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q59/p1", "position": "It attaches to 'you store' and locates what they hid privately.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī attach it to the latter verb, with no competing governance; al-Biqāʿī says a house is the most concealing personal place."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q60", "question": "How is buyūtikum vocalized?", "turns_on": "Ḍamma versus kasra on bāʾ.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q60/p1", "position": "The base reading has ḍamma on bāʾ, buyūtikum.", "reasons": "Qirāʾāt ER calls this canonical base."}, {"id": "3:49/q60/p2", "position": "A dialectal variant has kasra, biyūtikum.", "reasons": "Qirāʾāt ER says the vowel shift leaves meaning unchanged."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q61", "question": "Who speaks the closing statement?", "turns_on": "Jesus's continuous speech versus God's independent rebuke.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q61/p1", "position": "It continues Jesus's speech to the Israelites.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān prefers this because the clause is enclosed by Jesus's words; al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī allow it."}, {"id": "3:49/q61/p2", "position": "It is God's independent statement, reporting the proof and rebuking deniers.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān reports the rebuke analysis; al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī also allow God as speaker."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q62", "question": "How is the hamza in the closing inna read?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q62/p1", "position": "It has kasra, opening an independent assertion.", "reasons": "Abū Mālik specifies kasra and adds an unexplained 'if not' phrase."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q63", "question": "What does 'that' refer to in the closing statement?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q63/p1", "position": "All the preceding miracles, taken collectively as one set of signs.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn list bird-making, healing, revival and disclosure; Abū Mālik glosses 'that' as 'this'."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q64", "question": "How does 'if you are believers' qualify the sign?", "turns_on": "Future believers benefit, or existing believers are exhorted to sincerity and action.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q64/p1", "position": "The sign benefits those who believe or are receptive; disbelief blocks benefit, not its status as a sign.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī says knowledge of God as sender precedes recognizing the messenger; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the signs remain signs either way. {"id": "3:49/q65", "question": "What does 'believers' mean in the final condition?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q65/p1", "position": "Those who affirm the truth of God's messenger and accept his proof.", "reasons": "Saʿīd b. {"id": "3:49/q66", "question": "How do inward readings understand Jesus's signs?", "turns_on": "Literal acts versus spiritual education and regeneration.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q66/p1", "position": "The signs describe spiritual training: clay is an unformed soul, the bird its aspiration, breath divine knowledge, and cures purification.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī addresses prepared descendants of Jacob, reads blind as veiled, leprous as stained by vice and desire, and resurrection as knowledge. {"id": "3:49/q67", "question": "What do adjacent notes say God taught Jesus as Book and wisdom?", "turns_on": "Writing, another scripture, or broader knowledge and sound action.", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q67/p1", "position": "Book may mean handwriting; a report assigns Jesus nine of ten parts of writing.", "reasons": "Ibn Jurayj gives writing by hand; Jishumī reports the numerical division without a named authority."}, {"id": "3:49/q67/p2", "position": "Book may be another scripture besides Torah and Gospel, such as Psalms.", "reasons": "Abū ʿAlī prefers this as closer to the wording and prophethood."}, {"id": "3:49/q67/p3", "position": "Wisdom is knowledge or soundness of speech and action, including prophetic knowledge.", "reasons": "Jishumī reports both glosses and says Jesus knew Torah, Gospel and wisdom."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q68", "question": "How does this verse join the account of Mary and Jesus?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q68/p1", "position": "Mary's birth story pauses; the commentary turns to Jesus's mission, with the remainder of Mary's story in Sūrat Maryam.", "reasons": "Jishumī and al-Ṭabrisī give this narrative division."}, {"id": "3:49/q68/p2", "position": "The angelic promise was certain and fulfilled in Jesus's whole mission.", "reasons": "Elmalılı cites God's unbroken promise, the angels' truth, minhu and 'Be'; Jesus's life expressed the announced identity and call."}]}
{"id": "3:49/q69", "question": "Why did Jesus's signs match medicine, and how do other prophets' signs compare?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "3:49/q69/p1", "position": "God challenged each audience in its leading skill: Jesus's medicine, Moses's magic, Muḥammad's eloquence.", "reasons": "Jishumī says a miracle is conclusive when it defeats experts in their own field; Ibn Kathīr adds the Qur'an's inimitability before humans and jinn."}, {"id": "3:49/q69/p2", "position": "Moses's confrontation of Pharaoh and Jesus's Israelite challenge used visible signs before or apart from a new scripture.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī notes Moses's tablets came after Egypt, so the staff and hand answered Pharaoh; Jesus likewise came with signs."}]}
